claim: Ivkovic, Poterba and Weisbenner (NBER w10275, January 2004) compare a large discount broker's individual-investor trades in taxable versus tax-deferred accounts and find tax-loss selling throughout the calendar year, most pronounced in December and especially for investors who realized capital gains elsewhere in the portfolio, plus a capital-gains lock-in effect.
quote: Second, we find tax-loss selling throughout the calendar year, though it is most pronounced in December, particularly if the investor has realized capital gains elsewhere in the portfolio during the year.
limitations: Trade-level evidence only; gives no stock-price return size for a December-to-January rebound, and covers the 1990s before the growth of tax-sheltered accounts.
independent_replication: Corroborated by Grinblatt and Keloharju (Finland, same tax-loss pattern); no US post-2015 replication opened.
impact_on_spec: Defines the mechanism (tax-loss selling in December) but not the size; the size is what the ten-window test measures.

claim: Grinblatt and Keloharju (draft 2002-07-03, NBER w8745) find that Finnish investors realize losses more than gains toward the end of December and repurchase the sold stocks, producing net tax-loss buying pressure that is negative before the turn of the year and positive afterwards, and that turn-of-the-year returns, particularly for small firms, relate to that pressure.
quote: This trading pattern generates net tax-loss buying pressure that is negative prior to the turn of the year and positive afterwards.
limitations: Finnish market with a different tax regime; 1990s sample; regression evidence, no tradeable long-only excess return net of costs.
independent_replication: Same direction as Ivkovic-Poterba-Weisbenner for US individuals; Kaul et al. 2025 find the effect also existed in 1874-1917 without income taxes.

claim: Schwert (NBER w9277) shows on CRSP data that the small-minus-large NYSE return difference in the first 15 calendar days of January was still reliably positive after publication (daily alpha 0.00641, t 9.87, 1962-2001; 0.00565, t 5.37, 1990-2001), while the small-firm premium overall was much smaller after 1982 than in 1926-1982.
quote: Keim (1983) and Reinganum (1983) showed that much of the abnormal return to small firms (measured relative to the CAPM) occurs during the first two weeks in January.
limitations: Size spread, not year-to-date losers; ends in 2001; the fading after 2001 is not measured.
independent_replication: Keim (1983) and Reinganum (1983) are the original results; the JFIR 'revisited' paper reportedly finds fading later (claim_only).
impact_on_spec: Prior for the calendar window; does not license a loser tilt.

claim: Kaul, Mehrotra, Morck and Phillips (EFMA 2025 working paper) document a 3.1 percent January price increase in NYSE stocks over 1874-1917, before income taxes, and find larger January returns for small stocks, stocks with capital losses, illiquid stocks and volatile stocks, pointing to arbitrage costs as the reason the effect persists.
quote: Second, we find that returns are larger for stocks with the highest arbitrage costs: small stocks, stocks with capital losses, illiquid stocks and volatile stocks.
limitations: Historic sample before income taxes and modern institutions; not a 2016-2026 estimate; working-paper draft.
independent_replication: Consistent with Roll (1983) as cited by the authors; no independent replication opened.
impact_on_spec: Explains why the ADV top 1,500 restriction and the 2-6-12 bp cost tiers may leave little effect; supports running the 501-1,500 pool variant.

claim: McLean and Pontiff (October 2012 working-paper version of the JF 2016 article) study 82 published return predictors and find that the average post-publication decay, attributed to both statistical bias and price pressure from aware investors, is about 35 percent, larger for anomaly portfolios of large, liquid stocks.
quote: The average post-publication decay, which we attribute to both statistical bias and price pressure from aware investors, is about 35%, and statistically different from both 0% and 100%.
limitations: Average across 82 characteristics; the January-loser effect is not singled out.
independent_replication: Published version JF 2016; used elsewhere in this repository.
impact_on_spec: Supports the low prior; no design change.

claim: Anderson, Gerlach and DiTraglia (William and Mary WP 15, March 2005) find in two laboratory auction environments that prices in the January markets were systematically higher than those in December, suggesting a psychological contribution to the January effect.
quote: After controlling for variables that could influence subjects’ bids such as differences in private values, cumulative earnings, and learning effects, the prices in the January markets were systematically higher than those in December.
limitations: Lab experiment; no market data; no return size for a stock strategy.
impact_on_spec: None on the design; reported for completeness.

claim: Quantpedia's January Effect in Stocks page describes the rule 'invest in small-cap stocks at the beginning of each January, stay invested in large-cap stocks for the rest of the year' with indicative 12.7 percent per annum on 1947-2007 source-paper data (Easterday, Sen, Stephan), and states the strategy is long-only equity factor exposure, not a hedge.
quote: Invest in small-cap stocks at the beginning of each January.
limitations: Aggregator page summarizing an SSRN paper; no post-2007 numbers; not a loser-selection rule.
impact_on_spec: Confirms no ready-made 2016-2026 loser-rebound record exists to reuse.

claim: Globe and Mail (2025-12-11), search summary only, body paywalled: TSX stocks down more than 15 percent year to date underperform by nearly 4 percent from mid-November to mid-December and outperform by 3.6 percent from mid-December to mid-January.
limitations: Paywall; Canadian sample; practitioner summary; not opened, so not used as an effect size.
impact_on_spec: None; motivates the low prior only.

claim: JFIR 'Tax-loss selling and the January effect revisited', search snippet only (HTTP 403 on fetch): reports the January effect fading, likely because of more tax-sheltered accounts.
impact_on_spec: None; motivates the low prior only.
